segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I appreciate y’all coming here. As we begin, let me tell you the reason we are doing this. They are children learning here and on this side are young adults. They are going to start listening to Cherokee conversation to learn how to fluently speak Cherokee and also your family or if you have grandchildren. Someday, when you pass away, they may want to hear you talking - they will be allowed to listen to you talking. As we begin, tell me your full names in English.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: In Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In English first.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Betty Nofire is my name.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And you?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Eugene Nofire.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Qwedvyi.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Qwedvyi.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Qwudvdaw.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Qwudvdaw. Where were you born?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: I was born in Tahlequah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: At the old (hospital)?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: The same.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And where did you grow up?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Me? Do you know where they call it Fog Hollow?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, I know where it’s at.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Towards that way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was it like there? How many were in your family?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Just two, four. Well, Mom and Dad, and also there was just two of us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was it like for you children there growing up?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Like what?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Like, for instance, nowadays what children have to play with.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: No, it was not like that. We just made balls ourselves, made from socks and played ball. Sometimes when we found a doll, we would use the head and play with it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You all played ball with that.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, then when someone would look for it, nobody knew where it went.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you? Where did you grow up?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: On the mountain. They say Oak Ridge is where I grew up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many were in your family?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Let’s see, in all, there were nine of us children.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was it like for you growing up?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: It was also the same. We had it hard. For instance, just like she said, we didn’t play with anything got from the store. Just like she said, we played around just ourselves. We would climb trees and different things. We played with tires or threw horseshoes - different things growing up. I didn’t know what was outside. We didn’t have a TV or electricity. We were separated. You would say, where we came from.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did other people live close by?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, there were houses. There were lots of people living there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it just mostly family?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, all of us were a group in the Oak Ridge community. We were all related.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In Cherokee, your last name is Nuwotvni.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, that’s it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did your dad do to help provide for y’all?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: He worked in the woods back then, stables, I don’t know what they call it in Cherokee, and also he cut logs and posts from locust trees and different things. He did things like that. He never worked anywhere else until towards the last where they loaded chickens - he got involved in that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did he make what they call ties?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, he made things like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they use an axe back then, or what?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: No, he worked for some white man named George Brown, and he gave him a saw, a chainsaw, and he used his truck to haul. And he had a saw mill. He would take them there and they would make ties there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They would sell them there?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about your mom?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: She didn’t work to make money.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She just watched the house.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: All the time, as we were growing up, she watched us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you, what did your dad do?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: As far as I know, those ties. He worked by the railroad tracks, as far as I know, and also, like he said, he cut locust posts and sold them and used to buy food.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you all remember how much they got paid for them back then?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: They never looked back then. They would not tell you anything. You grew up as child and they themselves were the adults. The same went for their conversations. You could not listen. They would say, “Move away, you are a child, you don’t know anything.” Just like it is nowadays - if adults are talking and a child comes, they know more. Back then, they would get on to you and tell you to move away.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They would tell you to go play.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, they would say, “You are just a child.” We never knew how much they were getting paid for those ties, but I just know that is where he worked.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Back then, they picked strawberries and beans. Did you all do that?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, but in just a little while it ran out, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, I had picked up there. It was some Hume woman.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, she was partners with that Brown. I was saying they were partners. Anne Hume was her name.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, that was who it was. Where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Well I went to school at Zion. I went to school there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you finish there?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes. No, Dad went to Dallas. We lived there. I was in about the eighth grade when we came back, but I did finish there at Zion.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you go to high school?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: I went to Stillwell just for a little while. I didn’t like it - I was getting lonesome. I told my mom. She said if you can find another school I will go there. She said, “I will send you to Sequoyah if I talk to Ray??” So I went there, but something happened. The old lady got sick and I came back. Then for the rest of it I finished at Cave Springs.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So you finished there. When you first started school, were you already able to speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: They were getting on to me all the time ‘cause I could not understand English.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They were getting on to you for talking.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, I didn’t know what they were saying. I didn’t understand. All I knew was Cherokee. They would get on to you.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they have anyone appointed to help you all?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, it was someone - I don’t know the man’s name there, and there was an old lady there, if I would tell him he would tell them. I had a rough time at first, reason being they didn’t speak English growing up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: I went to school at Oak Ridge. In sixth grade at Bell they moved it from Oak Ridge. They closed it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you, did you already speak English?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Still today barely, they will be looking at me not knowing what I am saying. There at Oak Ridge we were all Cherokees. There was one white person. Sometimes they would get on to him ‘cause he didn’t understand. He understood more Cherokee. Our teacher, we all had one teacher.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You all were different ages.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: You mentioned they moved Oak Ridge school. When did they move it - what year was it?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: I don’t know if it was ‘70 or ‘71. Sometime, I don’t know, it was about that time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you finish at Bell or not?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: No, I got bored and quit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you quit there, what did you do?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Do you know Robert Swake? They loaded chickens.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: I helped him, that’s what I did. That’s what I did for 50 years.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Gaw!

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: My back gave out, so I had to quit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you retire?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you? When you finished at Cave Springs, what did you do?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Oh, really, I just worked everywhere. The canning factory and the chicken plant at Bentonville, I worked there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about when you lived in Dallas? Did you like it?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, it was good, but it was a big school. They were all different, like Spanish and other tribes of natives, you know, and all that were going to school there. It was good - I made it through OK.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about living there? What was it like?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: I was getting lonesome. I didn’t like it in a place like that. I would rather be in the country where my heart is.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So you wanted to come back.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, that’s it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many children do y’all have?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Three boys, two girls.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do they speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: The oldest one can speak but the youngest ones can’t.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They can’t? Y’all don’t speak Cherokee as much to those younger ones?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: We talk to them, but they don’t understand, and since about a year, I have begun talking to our grandchildren, trying to teach them. I realize I have made a mistake when I grew up, like she said. When we got to Bell it was the same, we did not speak English. It was all Cherokee. It was hard. It is just like us in here. If a Spanish person walks in here and talks to you, you won’t understand what they are saying to you. It was like that to us, but we had to learn. Even nowadays I still have not learned it all. I can understand those small words, but the bigger words I can’t. I don’t know the meaning. That is why we tried with those children for that not to happen to them. Back then they would get on to you and call you ignorant. Well, they are telling the truth, ‘cause we did not understand. That is why we taught our children like that, but I guess we went too far. And now we try to talk to our grandchildren.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Just that ignorant. It is not bad saying that, just someone not knowing, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, that is it. Not being able to understand.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We are all ignorant because we don’t know everything. Did your dad plant a garden?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: No he didn’t plant a garden. Toward the last, when I had already moved, he planted a garden.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did he make a good one?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: He made it pretty good then. I was never around. A white man was helping him. I had already left.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about your dad, did he plant a garden?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Not really, but my grandpa planted a garden. When we wanted something, we would go ask for it over there. He would give it to us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all have electricity hooked up back then?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Me, no.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: I didn’t.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Both of you didn’t.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: We didn’t have water coming inside until they started making wells.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So they didn’t make the water come all the way into the house.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: No, but when they put a pump outside, they put it on the inside. There was a ye-big [handle] sitting on top. When you pumped it on the outside, it would fill up. It was just for the sink to wash dishes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do y’all remember when y’all first got a TV?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: As for me, it wasn’t until we were already married. As for the other neighbors, they had them. If we wanted to watch something, we would go over there. Even if it was a radio you put batteries in, they would have one. Also a record player you put batteries in, they would just use those.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you like where you grew up at?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Me? Yeah, if I could, I would go back there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You don’t live there now? Or do you still live there?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: No, not where I grew up. We don’t have land. We didn’t have any land there. We couldn’t ,so we had to look in a different place.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where do you y’all live now?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Do you know where they call it (asda) Pevine?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: You know he was a counselor, that Crittenden?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Just over there, we are about a mile and a half apart.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But do you go to Oak Ridge church?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, do you know Diane Kelly?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: We live close together.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is she a good neighbor?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: I guess so. She waves when we see each other somewhere.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you learn to cook?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: My mother taught me and my grandmother would teach me. They first taught me to make bread. They taught me everything. They would stand me up on a chair and I would bake, I guess they were biscuits. I would make them huge, this big. But they would eat them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it a wood-burning stove?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes it was.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it the same for you?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: The same.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If you had to choose now which one you were going to eat from, which would you prefer?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: The other day I was telling him I would want a wood cook stove. We would put it aside in the shed to cook beans on. I was telling him the other day, if I can find one I would want one.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: It is better, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, it’s true.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: It is different.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: You don’t know of one.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s it. Me too, the same with heat to keep warm. I would want that instead, but...

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They want a high price for those stoves. I was at an auction in Proctor where they had one. When they first mentioned a price, they bidded it at $5,000, but nobody raised their hand. When they got to $500, we almost fought over it, but how much was it? They paid $850 for it.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Good happened to you.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: *unintelligble*

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When y’all started at Bell, y’all had both white and Cherokee mixed.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, half were white and half were Cherokee. There were mostly Cherokees from Sally Bull. Just some were from other places.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: All of your family that lived in Oak Ridge, do y’all not live there anymore?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: White man is the only one that has his own property and lives there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s probably good to hunt there.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: It used to be, but now the white man is coming and buying it. Now it says, ‘no trespassing.’ That’s what they call it when the game warden buys it. They bought it. As for me, I was glad. Reason being, you can still go there, and on this side there is government land, and you can still go there and toward where Grandpa and Grandma grew up, a white man bought it. I don’t know what he is going to do. They have land there, and in the middle he bought that there is a road there. I don’t know if he is going to close it. I don’t know what he is going to do, but if he closes it...

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: A white man does that everywhere.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: That’s it. That is what they told one. When we were working, he told him when he is talking about Satan, “You white people are Satan. Y’all control everything, y’all tear everything up, y’all want things to be your way. It’s y’all that the Bible talks about,” he told him. He didn’t like it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you really think about what you have come through compared to now, a lot has changed, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: (wulistvwe) Extremely.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you think about it, what has changed the most?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Love, it’s love. Back then, they watched each other or if someone was sick, they helped out. Nowadays, you will be sitting by yourself somewhere. As for me, I would say it’s love. It has all changed, but the most important thing is love.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you think about growing up, what do you miss about what you been through?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Well, it’s individual, but I would say freedom nowadays. Back then when I started driving a car, things were not the way they are now. All it was, is if you got in and had a license you could go anywhere. Now you can’t. You can’t now, everything has changed and also, you could go too far if you talked about things. Everything has changed as we go forward.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s full of the white man’s ways, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: That’s it. And it continues. I tell her, this one sitting here, “Let’s teach them to love one another.” Us Cherokees don’t love each other anymore. I was telling her there will be a group here that will be your relatives, and they will choose that side over there. They will put you outside. Us Cherokees don’t love each other anymore.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If you go any further, they will choose the white man’s side.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: That’s what I am saying, they are taking that side. I was watching old movies, like westerns and all, that he will be an Indian. He is just an Indian, they will say, and kill him quickly in the movies, ain’t it? And the director that has made them or whoever, that is the way he feels on how he looks at us natives, I was thinking. We stand here and want to be like he is and he looks at us that way I was thinking. I just think that to myself, but I just keep quiet inside.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It gives the feeling he is worth nothing but to be killed.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Just like a wild animal.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You said your dad did not plant a garden, but did y’all use things from the woods?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Like, say, medicine?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Onion, things to eat, onion, mushrooms.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Onion, poke salad, yeah. Toward the last, he did plant a garden. Like I was saying, he planted a lot, but I had already left. I moved from home a long time ago. This September, we will have our 50th anniversary we have been married. Back then, she was still in high school in the 11th grade. We have been together that long. when I moved out of the house, then I never went back. We were on our own and continue I don’t know for how long. Sometimes she gets on to me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all are ahead of me by three years.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: It’s been that long, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It became 47 in December. You mentioned medicine when you were growing up. For instance, if you had an ear ache or headache, did your dad use something for medicine?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, they had some by speaking. They would get close. I didn’t know what they were saying. They never taught me, and with tobacco or cigarette, they would blow smoke or use a straw or use something to blow inside. That was good. If we had a cold, we would just use a tree bark, and also grass like blueberry, they called just different things. We don’t go to the hospital even nowadays.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all still use things like that.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, I don’t know how. As for being sick, I couldn’t tell you when the last time I have been to the hospital. I was working and I did something to my back. I did go then, but I was not sick. It was to get shots of steroids I was looking for.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He did use fire sometimes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, if it was for tonsils, they used fire (coals). They would do that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about water? Did they blow that?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, if you had a fever. Fever they call it, they would blow that on you and you could feel that hot water dripping down. It would start from your head and it would get better. They all know things like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t pick any of that up?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: They did not tell me the first time. I just learned some of the things. Towards the end, Mom told me about spider bites as well. She said, “You just say this.” I told her if you write it down for me because I am going to forget in a little bit. But she got sick, so she didn’t. Mom knew a lot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you? Did you all use things like that where you grew up?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, we still do today. What little we know we just use that as we walk this earth, and we just ask. And also, we ask Him for us to make it through good. I am thankful for that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did your parents preserve things back then?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, that is what they used to do.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you? Did you learn that?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: They were teaching me. I might… I believe I could can the cabbage. His sisters and me used to can cabbage and fix it. I can do that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They called it sourkraut.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, you have to add lots of salt.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My wife makes it.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Recently we didn’t make any.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: You didn’t.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No, because we were just waiting around not going to get it.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Cabbage.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When we got to Barids, it was already closed. We used to get the cabbage there. It was already closed. We could not find any then.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: When Dad was alive, me and the girls used to can the sisters, but when he left, I guess we just forgot all about it. We don’t now.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It is really helpful ain’t it?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is what got them through, ain’t it? Back then in the past. My wife really does that. She cans like jelly and makes things like that. When someone comes over from time to time, they will go home carrying jelly.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: I am going over there, tell her.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you fish quite a bit?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were you a fisherman?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Still today we go. My body is not like it was, but I take my grandchildren to the water now. They fish, but as for me, I just sit there and watch them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, are they liking it?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: We have a boy that is about nine. He likes going fishing. Sometimes I don’t feel like going, but we still go.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do they like the fish, to eat them?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Seems like it. They eat when they fry them for them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Will they eat food like that?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: They eat it when she cooks it for them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Some will not eat wild onion, I wonder about them.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: She cooked them some squirrels. They did not know what they were eating, but I’ll say they liked them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you just fry them or how did you do them?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: No, boiled them.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, dumplings.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You made dumplings.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: They really ate them.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: I have never ate a squirrel that was fried.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You haven’t? I don’t like them made into dumplings from squirrel, but rabbits I do like.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: For me, rabbits are the only thing. They fry, they boil the squirrels, they do deer meat the same way also.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you like that, too, deer meat?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Are there bears up there?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: That is what they say, I have seen them once on our way to church, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Four crossed the road.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were they cubs?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: One was full grown and three were little.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about hogs?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: They say there is a lot. I have not seen them. White and them hunt all the time, and they find them. They kill them sometimes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about the mushrooms we mentioned. Which one do you like the best?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: I guess just all of them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you find them?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, those hickory chickens and that owl, they call and sometimes that wishie, they call it, comes out somewhere.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about what they call morrels? Do y’all find them?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Not just here lately. I have not found them. It’s been a long time, a long time ago. Mostly just what they call white owl and hickory chickens they call them Just them mostly.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about, did y’all raise hogs?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: No, not me, but my grandpa did.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He raised some.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Grandpa used to have some sometimes, the late Columbus. We would just keep them for a little while. They would go into the woods somewhere. I don’t know if it was because they were not feeding them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is probably where the ones living in the woods came from.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Probably did, those are probably mine that are running around.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all kill them?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, they killed them. They ate them good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they scrape them, or did they skin them?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: They scraped some of them. They said they killed one you know, and they poured hot water on it. He said we had it laying on a board when they poured hot water on it. It got up and took off running. It was not all the way dead when they shot it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They just knocked it out when it was laying there.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Then they chased it around again. Anyone would run if you poured hot water on them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is true, at my aunt’s house they had one. On the porch, or it wasn’t really a porch, they just had some stairs there. It was coming there all the time, and my aunt was getting aggravated with it. At some point, she splashed it with hot water. It just had ears this long from where she burned it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about, did you help when they killed hogs?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: I didn’t, but when they cut it up, I did that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about the intestines?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: I liked them, but I didn’t like cleaning them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You like eating them tho.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, they are good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: As for me, I just like the little ones cut in small pieces and fried real hard. I don’t like the rest of it.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Me too, fried real hard, that is better.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Those are the only ones I like. Where y’all go to church now at Oak Ridge. Have you been going there since you were a child?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: I would go, but I was not a member. I would go every now and then toward the last, when we moved. Well, we moved to Fairfield, and there she came to the altar. Keith Ketcher was the pastor, and Raymond Glass. She was supposed to be baptized. They kept moving it, so we gave up and we went to Salem, and from Salem, Frank Acorn went to the pastor at Oak Ridge. We went there and surrendered. Since then, we are still there. When I was a child, I was one of those kids that just ran around there, but since we have grown up, we have been members there. Still today, we are still going.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is it all in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Well, the young adults, it’s the same - they don’t hardly understand. We try with both.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do y’all have quite a few?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: When we are doing something. There will be lots of children but there is just a few of us grown ups.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Us at Belfonte, we don’t have young adults.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, that is us, say for instance Christmas, there will be more or Easter or Sunday they will come, but here the past two weeks they are not hardly coming, just very few.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: I guess they are chasing a ball.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is true nowadays. When we were growing up, it would just be at the school, but now they go everywhere playing ball. One of my grandchildren finished. They are not going to school anywhere now. They were going everywhere. They would go as far as Texas playing ball, and me, we were just making noise in the woods.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: There were places back then, too, ain’t it, for some baseball players.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Wasn’t your dad a pitcher?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: That is what they say.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They say he had a strong arm, and I think they said he was a third baseman. I don’t know if it’s true.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: He said fourth, or that is what he used to say. He said people used to tell him, “Win your own ball game.” But I don’t know, they will tell you anything.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you were going to school at Bell, did you play basketball?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: We didn’t hardly know how up there. We didn’t have things like that. Just played softball. When we got to Bell, we did not know how to play basketball. They would put us in, but we didn’t know how it was. Just so we could rebound, that was all they wanted, but as for the rest, like for instance, we didn’t even know what a three-second lane was then, really.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all were just standing there.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: We were just standing there, fighting for the ball. When we got it, we threw it to our teammate, and they knew what to do with it. We didn’t have that at Oak Ridge. We were hillbillies when we got there. One time at Greasy, you remember, they had that wood floor at Greasy?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: He didn’t have any shoes, just his socks. They had waxed it. He was guarding them, waving his arms, sliding, going by and could not stop. We were funny, but we finished.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When I was going to school at Greasy, sometimes when the girls got finished, we would borrow the girls’ shoes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: That is the way it was for me. When we played, they gave me some tennis shoes this long. I was walking around like Donald Duck. I wasn’t able to run good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you were catching chickens, how many did y’all have to carry then?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: It was different, I guess you could say it was the old days when you had to carry them outside. We carried 15, we carried 11, and four. Then when they used a loader, a machine was running around, it was just a few like 13, 12 or just 10. It was easy, or it seemed like it then, but the first time we carried that many 4-pounders. Some had to carry 15 back and forth all night, and some to those really long buildings, the chicken houses. You would go get them with a cage at the head, and it would be 400ft where the truck was parked. You had to carry them all the way, and then go all the way back over there. It was hard work doing that, but we had to make a living. There was no place to get it, you had to work.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you got started, how long did it take y’all to finish one house?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Just different. Some they had were good, It would be easy, and some did not have side doors, so you had to carry them a long ways. If it was good, we would finish easy, and if they were bad a long time, you had to carry them a long ways. That wasn’t good. And sometimes we would start in the evening and would not get done till the next morning. All night we worked.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You said you done something to your back. Did that happen to almost all the chicken catchers?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: That’s what they say.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: It’s the same, like me now when I walk I have a shorter leg here. The side or back does something. I guess it is because it was heavy on one side from carrying them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you were living in Dallas, did they play ball like that, too?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: I don’t know, all I did was watch them play basketball.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t get involved.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: No, you know when they hang a ball and they hit this way I don’t know what the name is for that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Feather ball.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You have to hit it.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: They did that, but I did not get involved.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it just you, or were other Cherokees when you were living in Dallas?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: No, I don’t know. My dad was working at the airport. I think my mom. Mom got sick on us. She had to go to the hospital. I didn’t know the reason why we brought her all the way back here. But she brought a baby, but we didn’t know why. They didn’t, you know, would not tell you anything like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yesterday our youngest girl, you know where they call Crowley Texas, she is over there, lives there.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: As soon as she finished here at Sequoyah, she left. She has lived there that long, she comes to visit us sometimes, or we go visit her sometimes.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Two of our grandchildren’s grandmother’s relatives live there in Dallas. They go there sometimes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about y’all? Do you go there sometimes?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: We would get lost, we won’t see anything bigger than Stilwell.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is what happened to me there. We went to San Antonio. I said we will stop by my sister’s and see her, and we will do the same thing I told them. So we stopped by. We were going to go the same way, but I got lost in Dallas all night. They have a big race track this side. It was turning morning when I recognized that. I just said “Let’s go home.” We looked for my sister’s house all night.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: They are used to it, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, it is a big town. When you said your dad planted a garden, were there already things to use back then?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: No, they would use a shovel and pick to break the ground and the Jones, Vonnie Jones would plow it with a tractor. That’s what White said. He knows all of it because he and Dad lived close by. Me, we just go out that way on weekends. So when they did that for them, then they would use a tiller. I guess that is what they call that thing that goes around. But breaking it up, they used that other thing.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long did your dad pastor there at Oak Ridge?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Well it was 84 when he was ordained, but he was a licensed minister from 84 to 20 or 21 you could say.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: That was about it.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: It was about that long he pastored.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It was all in Cherokee, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, it was all in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Can you read Cherokee?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, if it’s the old ones. Those newer ones they made are a little harder. Some of it is a little different how it goes, but you can figure it out. But if it’s the old ones, I can understand it good. That is what we use in Cherokee in Sunday school to learn with.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We do the same thing.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: The same thing in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Can you also write in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: I can’t, I never have tried.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I am not able to write it either. I tried to when I was hired over there. It was Cherokee Nation. “If you can read Cherokee and can write it, we will give you a raise,” said a letter that came. I read it easy but then I had to write a little bit. I wrote a little bit, but no telling how long I took. They gave me a dollar raise.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: If that was it, just slow, but they would give up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I almost stayed in there all day just looking for a dollar. Is there quite a few in there that can read?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Let’s see, how many are there? I,2 there are about five, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, that youngest boy can read it, but he can’t speak it. I mean, he don’t understand all of it.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: He don’t know what he is saying. He uses too much English, there is White and Albert and a few of the women and both of us. We can read Cherokee, and one of our boys.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Are the others learning too, from reading those?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: I don’t know, they are always getting help. I don’t know, they can say some things but they cannot read it all.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I don’t know, there are about 13 that can read. They are really moving along learning. Someone will come at anytime and say, “What is this that is written? What is this word?” They seem to want to.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: That’s good, that is how we learned. We would go to Dad’s on the weekdays. He would teach us; by doing that we learned.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I tell them this: don’t just learn to read it, learn the meaning. It is good if they learn it that way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Does Levi go to visit y’all sometimes?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, he was helping us, but the last time, it was sad, he fell. You know how there is like stairs? When he stepped off it, he backed up but he landed sitting in the chair. If it wasn’t for that, he would have fell to the ground. So now we feel sorry for him there. He will not give up, but it’s sad.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He is forgetting things, I can tell.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, that is why we used to use him all the time just like he was OK, but when that happened to him the last time, we felt sorry for him.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Are you the pastor now?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Well I just have a license. Gary Flynn helps us, like for instance, Lord’s Supper or baptism, different things like that. Gary Flynn is there every Saturday night. He comes there all the time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do y’all have church every Saturday night?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, we are having church all the time. Sometimes there are just about eight of us, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: And sometimes 15. There are not very many of us. Most of them are moving. Half of them are in Fairfield that left from there. But it is good if they are in a church, then going back into the world. Yeah, we keep going.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is the singing all in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, the women use song books that are in English, but the songs we sing in all Cherokee. But we don’t sing a lot nowadays, like two, or Gary will lead two. Albert will sing two or three, and Gary will, and then just the women. We just go that far - we don’t sing a lot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It is the same way for us. Sometimes they will lead two or three, and then there is a group of women, they like to sing. Sometimes they will wave me over. They want me to lead some for them. That’s when we sing quite a few in Cherokee, and they are learning.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: That’s good, what about your brother Stanley, does he still sing?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He is not hardly able to go to church. He got sick. He had it cut off here.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Oh that’s what. Oh, OK,

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He is really sick. He could be in the hospital. Suddenly he has been having troubles. That group our family had that sung, we don’t do that anymore.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: I remember when y’all used to sing at Chucalate long time ago with your dad, too, ain’t it? (waleli)

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Mom used to really like to sing. She was funny, she used to put tobacco in her mouth. It would be dripping down while she was singing. She would just do it like this, and keep singing.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Nothing would interrupt her.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The older ones of the family would be lowering because they were embarrassed.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: That is what they will do, ain’t it, they will be embarrassed of you, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: But she wasn’t singing for them, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No, she didn’t care, she would not be interrupted by anything.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: They will say you are out of tune sometimes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I used to tell my family, when we had a good group someone from Lincoln was playing music for us, we sung for them at Muldrow, we sung one song we sang all the time called I’ll Fly Away. We were singing and it seemed different to me, when I noticed we were all singing a different verse. I said we are really good singers, we are all singing different verses.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Y’all finished very quickly.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, we were in Fayetteville one time, we sung that. A man asked if there was anyone else that wanted to sing, and so they raised their hand and said “I do” so he told them to come on. In English he said this. “I am going to sing that song the way that song they are singing is supposed to be sung.” He said, “I am going to sing how it should be sung. In English.” They call it a hobby. Does any of you have one?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Say for instance what?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: For instance, something you like doing or making.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: As for me, nowadays just mostly playing with my grandchildren. Sometimes I limp around, but that is what I like the most as far as doing anything else. At the house, the trampoline they call it or what do they call it, I lay close to where they come out, and when they say jump, I try to.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Their intention is to laugh at you, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: They will not do anything without duda. I told them we need four dudas. Duda here, duda, duda, duda.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You have to see what they are doing, ain’t it? Do they do you the same way?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: That is about it nowadays. I don’t do anything.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: We are supposed to pick one up here in a little bit in immersion. Is that it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Are they going to school?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, going to school here.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When they around you, do they talk?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: In Cherokee?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Not the little one. She is just a little girl, the one she is talking about.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, so not yet.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Over there where they babysit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh that’s it.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: It is there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is one of your sisters named Eva?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, that is her name. But we keep it a secret.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She would probably think and say the same thing, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Her and White are always at it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Does she still live up there or not?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: No she lives on this side of Salem.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Sometimes I see her at the auction.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s where she lives.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She will be there.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: You know where the community building is at Bell? Between there and Salem, the house in the middle, she lives there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is her husband’s name?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Monroe.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Monroe, ain’t it? There were some women that came a while ago, they were from Jay. If they are from Jay and also Belfonte, they really believe in Bigfoot that they talk about. What do y’all think?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: I am not going to believe it until I see it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They will tell you it is true.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Have they seen it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Some say they have seen it. I would not say you are lying because I don’t know.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: If I see it I will believe it, because I don’t know, I really don’t know.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I don’t want to see something like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about what they call little people?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: It was a long time ago, for the reason being I don’t know if it was that. But when I was growing up, you know where Columbus used to live?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: There is a road, then it goes like this. There was a house and another road went this way. There would be a car, a vehicle coming, you could hear it good, and right before it came out there, it would turn quiet, and then it would start back up way over there somewhere. And the elders would say, “It is those little people.” I didn’t see that so I don’t know if it is true. But I did hear that for myself, but I did not see them. It could have been something else, but I never have seen one driving a car. I don’t know where they would have got one. I guess they bought it somewhere. But it would do that like it was going to come out any minute. They would be looking, it would turn quiet, and then start back way over there somewhere. That is just what they would say, but I have never seen one, that is just what they would say. I don’t know if I believe it. But I would not believe it until I see it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They say they will get you lost.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: That is what I have heard, that is what I have heard.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I don’t know if you know Johnny Sanders was his name.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: (Godvwasgi) yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: (Godvwasgi) they say they got him lost. They caught him, they used to say. But his self, he never mentioned anything like that.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Now what I was saying about Bigfoot, it’s been about two months ago. Do you know where the rider Daugherty is?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Someone was coming there, walking. It was one of those Sevenstar boys coming, and as he came across the road something made a noise on this side, so he looked. He was saying something tall with red eyes was looking at him. He said he kept walking and it followed him for some ways. Then the road did this. It went straight and it went the other way, he was saying when he was telling them about it.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: In the day or at night?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: At night. I don’t know, but they had a statue of one they made there at Belfonte, and they would move it around. It would be in one field when we would go by on Sunday, and the next Sunday it would be in another. That is the way they were doing it. He may have seen that, I was thinking.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Do you remember, did you know Tom Neugine?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I have heard of him.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: He used to live underneath that Baron Bridge. He was telling us that he seen Bigfoot. He said he was cleaning up at the water, and it jumped towards him, and he had shorts on, and he was eating crawdads, but he was lying.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He was wearing shorts.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: That is what he said.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: He probably let him borrow it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We have a seven year old boy that we have been given (adopted) and also a girl that is eight years old. They were talking about that one time, and the boy was listening. When they got finished he got quiet. I am going to say what he said in English. He said, “Pa, you know that Bigfoot?” I said what he told me, he has only one foot. I said, “Yeah.” He said, “Yeah, because if he two feet, they would be calling him Bigfeet.” I was wondering how much he thought about.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: What about this? When I was growing up, the adults and the elders, we would be at the stomp grounds( gateyo). I just knew their names in Cherokee. I never did think about it till recently. I wonder what they call them in English, because I just know their names in Cherokee. It is interesting that I never learned their names in English. Was it like that when you were growing up?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Not really that much. There is a lot of things she can say in English that I can not say in Cherokee, and it’s hard. That is just my opinion on things like that. I guess we are just not given everything to say, I don’t know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you see family members, do you speak in all Cherokee?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: When we see each other?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Yes, just both in Cherokee and in English. The one that is doing the baptizing, and if the one that is getting baptized does not understand Cherokee, he talks to him in English so they can understand real good. But if it is just us, we all speak in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you and your family? When you call one another’s name, do you call each other in Cherokee or in English?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: In English.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: At Belfonte, they use lots of Cherokee when they call one another.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: For instance, us growing up they say nickname. We just used that to call each other.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We are going to finish now. The way we speak Cherokee now, what do you think is going to happen to it?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: Possibly the way I understand it is if we do not make an effort, it is going to pass away for the reason being that white man: that has taught Cherokee, it is different the way I understand it. Some he says it right, but some he writes it different from the way I understand it, because if we do not teach them ourselves, I will say it is going to pass away. If we fight, you can say it is in our hands now on. What we are going to do if we walk out and forget, it fades away slowly. But if we walk out and teach them, it will keep going. The way I understand it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you?

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: I think the same way, for reason being where I work we are teaching them Cherokee, but for instance it is different. the teacher will ask me what I think. I will say that is not the way I would say it is. (Tsisdetsi) mouse, that is just how we speak it. I was telling them. That is what I am saying (geyunegi) she agrees with me about things when I am teaching. She will tell them, “I believe her.” They asked her if she understood Cherokee when they were talking to her and she said yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: For me when we say (tsisdetsi) they are going to say (tsisdetsi).

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, that is what I am saying. Why, when we take them to the Cherokee bowl, when they say (tsisdetsi) they put an x in it. Not until they say (tsisdetsi), then they count it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They pass them.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Why is it like that?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is where they are mixing the English I believe.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: When they do that, if you write (tsisdetsi) you cannot just make the G sound, you have to write the tsi. That is the reason they do that. But at this school, what would you say if they have symbols written to say all of it tsi or gi or gi sound? That is the way they have it nowadays. But that is how they do it. But how would you say it? But as I was growing up, everyone knew me. They used to call me Mitchy, the reason being my grandmother knew my name in English. She would say “Mitchi.” They learned from her. It is kind of about what you were saying (tsisdetsi). I can say the same thing (tsisdets) but if you write it, you have to write (tsisdetsi). That is why they put it on there in the challenge bowl. But I guess we have to decide for ourselves how the young children are going to learn that the reason for the way that they do that, from what I understand. But as for me, I tell my children and also my grandchildren what they should do.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I went to school there at North Eastern. I was learning Cherokee. Sometimes some of us would have a spelling test and I would draw a picture of a tsisdetsi, and I would write tsisdetsi, and he would read them. He would knock it off (tsusdetsi) tsi I say I take the tail off. They gave me the lowest grade. In two weeks, I was reading all of it. Then the others, I was standing way ahead of the others. But when I spelled it like gitle dog, they would knock it off. That English was bothering him.

segments.speaker: betty-nofire
segments.translation: Yeah, me too when they say tsisdetsi, I don’t say tsisdetsi, but when they have to go there, I say it will be better if you will say this.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: What about when they are saying hi? Some will say siyo the way I have heard from the elders. They would say osiyo, they would make it longer. Nowadays they make it shorter, the way it is. Have you heard them saying osiyo before?

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: No, just siyo.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Is that right, you just heard siyo? That is the way the elders said it was osiyo.

segments.speaker: eugene-nofire
segments.translation: For instance, the way I understand it, if there is a community here and another community there, there is a little difference in the way we say it, but we understand one another. But the white man wants us to learn the full way to say it. Even for us, we would just say siyo where I grew up like I said. If it is in a different place, they say osiyo. If I say, “Oh I’m just hurting somewhere” I was telling them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I appreciate that y’all came.
